title: 📖 02 — Peoples & Cultures
rawNotionMarkup: Edition II continuity and provenance note. This chapter is the complete available Notion reference from 20 November 2026, retained as the detailed starting text rather than condensed. It remains revisable by its creator. Review the evidence-status guardrails below; the original Bible and chat export may provide later additions. ## Era of Fire — third and final era of the Second Age, 116 years (creator canon, 21 November 2026) AVARRAN HISTORICAL NAME, CREATOR-ESTABLISHED: The third and final Avarran-defined era of Eryndor's Second Age is called the Era of Fire; other continents may name or divide the period differently. It lasted 116 years, corresponding to Second Age Years 1,322–1,437 inclusive. Its exact duration is derived from the already confirmed Second Age total: 1,437 − 321 years (Era of Awakening) − 1,000 years (Era of Wonder) = 116 years. Chronology: (1) Era of Awakening, Years 1–321, 321 years; (2) Era of Wonder, Years 322–1,321, 1,000 years; (3) Era of Fire, Years 1,322–1,437, 116 years. The catastrophic global earthquakes at the end of the Era of Fire ended the Second Age and began the Third Age. Their causes, seismic effects, sudden marshland and lowland mountain uplift, tenfold global aftershock amplification through the ancient Ironspine, mass deaths without whole-species extinction and the as-yet-undefined magical protection are recorded separately, not invented here. CREATOR REVISION — HISTORICAL DEVELOPMENT NOW AUTHORIZED: The earlier prohibition against writing the Era of Fire's interior was superseded on 21 November 2026. Its cultures, regional kingdoms, wars, social movements and dark-mage events are now documented in the Second Age Annals and the dedicated Era of Fire chronicle. No First Throne involvement, new worldwide catastrophe, specific dragon cult or fire god is thereby established. The name Fire is an Avarran historical era name; its definitive etymology remains open. Gloin's ancestry and paused campaign remain unaffected. ## Edition II continuity guardrails - The nine additional intelligent peoples are established canon, even if earlier draft language says some descriptions are still being developed. Do not demote them to mere proposals. - Keep culture-specific reputations and potentially dangerous local encounters distinct from innate morality, cognition, universality or destiny. - No invented racial population/lifespan numbers or uniform political structures; respect unknown details and species distinctions. - The accidental proposed names Talarin, Khevari, Nerathi, Thallin and Cindari are explicitly not canon. - Drakari, Aelwyn, Ents, Giants, Living Mountains and intelligent animal peoples retain their established, non-interchangeable classifications. Direct source: Peoples & Cultures. Historical source: The Eryndor World Bible. --- ## Conflict, exploitation and enslavement across peoples Slavery and forced captivity exist in parts of Eryndor, but species is never a fixed moral or political role. Any intelligent people may include captors, victims, defenders, governments that prohibit slavery, governments that tolerate it, and communities of escaped people. Captors can exploit their own species or others, for economic, military, political, personal, customary or discriminatory reasons. No universal racial slavery pattern is mandated by the creator's example of an Urakai warlord capturing Khazari miners. This rule preserves the Urakai's political sophistication and all other peoples' individual and cultural diversity. Eryndor Living Atlas VII — Slavery, Bondage, Serfdom & Resistance distinguishes practices, provisional regional laws and competing factions. ## Regional cultures and subcultures — new complete living-culture expansion Explicit creator rule: Every intelligent people has multiple cultures; every region contains overlapping local subcultures. The distinctive Khazari idea that contribution earns respect is not a generic value imposed on Eldar, Urakai, Halflings, Centaurs, Merfolk, Goblins or other peoples. Each community has its own admired paths, kinship traditions, duties, taboos and dissenting individuals. Culture comes from species + continent + settlement + state + occupation + household + life experience, and shared multi-species village identity can override older labels. 1. Eryndor Living Culture Atlas VIII — Thrones, Eldar, Urakai, Humans & Elder Courts: Seven independent Khazari traditions, multiple Eldar/Urakai branches, five human power-group subcultures, Drakari and Aelwyn courts. 2. Eryndor Living Culture Atlas IX — Smaller Peoples & Regional Traditions: Halflings, Gnomes, Goblins, Ents, Centaurs, Merfolk, Giants, the nine later-established peoples, and guarded unknowns for Living Mountains. 3. Eryndor Living Culture Atlas X — Animal Peoples, Diasporas & Mixed Communities: Wolvenkin, Foxfolk, Lionfolk, Tigerfolk, Elephantfolk, Bearfolk, Cowfolk and Pigfolk, all with several regional alternatives. 4. Eryndor Living Culture Atlas XI — All Peoples by Continent & Regional Subcultures: 28 modeled peoples × 5 continents regional crosswalk, 28 distinct cultural zones among five continents, shared mixed-town and professional subcultures, and methods for generating persistent local variation. Authority: These are new, creator-revisable setting expansions, not recovered original history or dialogue. Old confirmed ethnic/political foundations and Gloin's story take priority. No birth rates, marriage ratios, offspring biology, family sizes, lifespans or population totals change. Big families and centuries-long craft pursuits coexist, and no NPC gains world knowledge automatically. Current in-game time remains Autumn Day 22, Year 3,847, 11:25 AM. ## Khazari social norm — family choice, craft mastery and the duty to contribute Creator-established Khazari cultural principle: Marriage, children and mastery of a craft are independent dimensions of a dwarf's life, and none of their combinations is inherently strange or shameful. Some Khazari are legendary masters who also raise substantial families. Others live with partners and children while being perfectly competent, ordinary craftspeople without pursuing perfection. Others devote centuries to becoming masters and never form a family. Some do not choose mastery but still do honest work, maintain friendships and households, and contribute to their communities. Being unmarried, childless, married, highly skilled or unexceptional in one's trade is not itself grounds for stigma. The real cultural expectation is useful effort: A Khazari who is capable of contributing yet deliberately chooses permanent idleness and expects others to carry their burden may face disapproval, gossip and loss of respect. Dwarven culture values work, effort, service, responsibility and craft, not just extraordinary talent. A reliable journeyman, farmer, trader, clerk, cook or parent can be respected alongside a master engineer. Apprenticeship, study, running a household, raising children, caring for relatives, public service and community duties count as meaningful work; contributing need not mean wage employment or physically strenuous labour. Fairness and individual variety: Illness, disability, injury, involuntary unemployment, bereavement, age, recovery and genuine difficulty finding work are not equivalent to choosing laziness. Different Khazari individuals and clans may judge people more harshly or more generously, and a town can have internal debates about inherited wealth, early retirement or what counts as service. These are social expectations, not compulsory species instincts or a universal criminal law. Long lives and demographics: Overlapping generations and large extended families remain integral to Eryndor. Mastery and family may coexist for centuries. No birth rates, fertility biology, populations, marriage ratios or character ages change. Tolkien's isolated or unmarried craft-absorbed Dwarves are one possible archetype, not a general rule imposed on the Khazari. Gloin-specific continuity: Gloin Hammerfeld, 42, is recorded as not employed and not enlisted at the Day 19 opening, but he is actively pursuing work, instruction, research and a direction in life. Do not narrate that his family or society has branded him lazy merely because his employment status was unset; reactions require dialogue and actual behaviour in play. His family Durgan, Mara, Bruni, Tovin and Elska remains unchanged. ## Long-lived peoples — preserve large family dynamics Creator correction — large families remain central: Long lives and deep personal obsessions do not imply small households, weak kinship or scarce children as a universal feature of Khazari, Eldar or any other species. Eryndor already contains large, layered family networks: multiple siblings, parents, grandparents, ancestors, cousins, extended clans and generations whose lives overlap for decades or centuries. Some people pursue work and family simultaneously; other individuals choose solitude, courtship later or no children. An engrossed craftsperson can be a devoted parent, grandparent, sibling or clan elder. Neither a general marriage rate nor any birth/fertility rate is being newly specified or changed. Concrete existing proof: The ordinary working-class Hammerfeld household includes father Durgan (168), mother Mara (161), and four children: Bruni (57), Gloin (42), Tovin (34) and Elska (26). This family structure and its Day 21 supper are established story canon, not newly proposed worldbuilding. Don't shrink that family, change anyone's ages, or infer absence of kinship because a Tolkien comparison discussed unmarried Dwarves. A multi-century clan may span several simultaneous generations while birth-rate assumptions remain exactly as previously established. ## Long-lived peoples — mastery, private pursuits and changing life priorities Creator's cultural direction, 21 November 2026: Long lifespans can encourage many Khazari, Eldar and other long-lived peoples to become deeply engrossed in their own pursuits—craft, scholarship, song, inventions, politics, gardens, exploration, beauty, private philosophy, family heritage or personal projects—over decades or centuries. Some choose not to marry or have children; some have families earlier in life and later devote themselves to other interests. This offers social depth and a qualitative cultural explanation for why long lives do not automatically produce rapid population growth. No established birth rate, reproductive capacity, demographic ratio or population total is being changed or invented. Real fictional-literary comparison (inspiration, not copied Eryndor biology): Tolkien's Dwarves include many who remain unmarried because their crafts occupy them; see The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A, “Durin's Folk,” summarized at [Tolkien Gateway: Dwarves](https://tolkiengateway.net/wiki/Dwarf). Tolkien's Eldar tend to have children during an earlier period and turn later toward arts and other matters; see Morgoth's Ring, “Laws and Customs among the Eldar,” summarized at [Tolkien Gateway: Elven life cycle](https://tolkiengateway.net/wiki/Elven_life_cycle). “Elves become selfish and forget family” is not a faithful universal summary; changes in desire and priorities are not equivalent to selfishness. These Tolkien-specific mechanics are not automatically Eryndor's reproductive laws. Eryndor cultural interpretations (examples, not universal rules): - Khazari: A maker may apprentice for decades, refine a tool or forge method for a century, maintain a family's workshop across dynasties, or devote a lifetime to a mine, mountain-hall, public works or archive. Marriage, kinship and raising children can remain important alongside work; some characters prefer craft or autonomy. A personal obsession can be admirable, eccentric or destructive. - Eldar: A painter may take 120 years to finish a tapestry, a linguist devote centuries to lost scripts, a court diplomat keep negotiations alive across mortal reigns, or a gardener shape trees over generations. Many still love, raise children or protect their families; individual attitudes differ. - Other long-lived peoples: An Ent's stewardship, Giant clan elder's memory, Drakari court's accumulations and Aelwyn otherworldly interests can produce different concepts of ambition or family. Their exact reproduction is species-specific and remains unresolved where the original Bible did not specify it. - Variation and dramatic tension: Some ancient scholars become brilliant and benevolent; some become isolated, jealous, proud, self-absorbed or unwilling to change. Some love raising large families if consistent with their species and established life history. No people's personality or morality is fixed by age alone. Much shorter-lived neighbors may find a five-decade project baffling or insulting. Demographic and campaign constraints: Preserve the established 24m Khazari, 18m Eldar, other Atlas population estimates, and the creator's explicit birth-rate freeze. Never invent low birth rates, changed sex ratios or new reproductive biology by citing Tolkien. Do not force Gloin, his relatives, Maela, Hadrik or any named character to renounce marriage/family or adopt an obsession unless supported in play. Ancient cultures may be sophisticated, stable, dynamic, generous, decaying or conflicted without compulsory stagnation. ## Recovered original premise — numerous peoples without unified kingdoms An out-of-character discussion between the creator and the earlier narrator explicitly established that political sophistication does not require a single monarchy, unified state or imperial capital. The following are established intelligent peoples with the stated common population patterns; the broad descriptions must not be imposed as compulsory traits on every individual or settlement. | People | Original social and geographic description | | --- | --- | | Halflings | Numerous across human territories, including farmers, craftspeople, merchants and traders, with extensive kin networks, prosperous rural settlements, and some halfling-majority regions. No single unified Halfling kingdom; peaceful reputations do not make them politically powerless. | | Ents / Elderwood | Ancient, intelligent tree-like peoples, usually in old-growth forests; extremely long-lived and potentially thousands of years old. Generally uncommon; organised around ancient groves and gatherings rather than conventional cities or kingdoms. Some move, fight or converse with other peoples; an Ent gathering can wield major influence. | | Gnomes | Numerous in cities and often living alongside humans, Khazari and Eldar; associated with invention, alchemy, mechanics and scholarship. Maintain independent communities and urban guild connections without one great unified kingdom. | | Goblins | Numerous on multiple continents; diverse settlements, trading networks, confederations and some urbanised centres. Often include miners, scouts, traders and craftspeople. Relations vary; Goblins and Urakai are distinct peoples. | | Centaurs | Primarily grassland and open woodland; mobile clans or confederations without a permanent unified kingdom; skilled in warfare, archery and tracking. | | Merfolk | In major seas and coastal waters; inhabited underwater settlements, trading routes, diplomatic relations with some surface civilisations, and diverse polities including independent city-states. | | Giants | Relatively uncommon in remote mountains and northern regions; solitary individuals and isolated clans, with ancient traditions and significant physical strength. | Principle explicitly stated in the original chat: These are not “lesser races” or inferior civilisations. Different peoples may organise economic, legal, cultural, diplomatic and social life without a conventional kingdom. Their broad generalities are not moral rankings, absolute universal temperaments or reasons to deny them deep individual histories. Other canon peoples not mentioned in this particular source are not thereby excluded. This exchange was worldbuilding outside the campaign and did not advance Day 19's in-world clock or constitute information learned by Gloin. ## New patchwork-town social design — shared citizenship across species Eryndor Living Atlas VI — Patchwork Villages & Folktale Crossroads establishes several new multi-species villages and towns, led by Bramblebridge with \~3,600 residents belonging to 18 already-established intelligent peoples, sharing public institutions, food markets, housing, work and neighborhood disputes. This implements the owner's desired ensemble-fairy-tale atmosphere without copying particular fictional characters or adding Mousefolk as a new sapient species merely by analogy. Some towns are unusually welcoming; others contain real prejudices, crime, predators, class differences and serious danger. The same species can occupy an unfamiliar region by migration, trade and settlement, and no single species has a predetermined moral nature. All details new and revisable. ## Sixfold world census is now the current baseline — 21 November 2026 Population resimulation completed: The creator explicitly accepted a 6× revision of previously simulated Year 3847 populations. The current modeled world total is 2,062.800 million residents (formerly 343.800m), with Avarra 1,019.760m, Tharvorn 171.000m, Sahrad 282.222m, Orundel 393.600m and Vaelora 196.218m. The 28-people by five-continent matrix, 133 previously quantified named settlement/Throne entries, the 18 resident categories of Bramblebridge, and the 8 other quantified patchwork places, plus habitat and carrying-capacity constraints, are audited in Eryndor Living Census XII — Sixfold Population & Carrying-Capacity Audit. Priority and supersession: All old 343.8m, 24m Khazari, 22m Seven Thrones, 18m Eldar, 31m Urakai and 3.8m Karak-Varn figures in the preserved legacy text are superseded as current demographic estimates by 6× figures. They remain intact only as historical reference or original simulation baselines. New: 144m global Khazari; 132m Seven-Throne domain subtotal included in the 144m; 22.8m Karak-Varn included in the Thrones. Do NOT add these overlapping totals. Long-lived peoples retain unchanged birth rates, and any specific community may still face housing, food, water and supply crises because the new populations are not equally concentrated. This is a historical-scale editorial resimulation, not 6× births during the current play session. No old ancient First Throne uncertain peak estimate or unnamed uncensused species is automatically multiplied. Gloin's Year 3847, Era of Crowns, Fifth Age campaign remains paused at Hadrik's desk, Autumn Day 22 \~11:25 AM. ## New living-world species distribution and population supplement Eryndor Living Atlas I — Continents, Habitats & Population Model models the geographic distributions of the 28 numeric resident peoples across Avarra, Tharvorn, Sahrad, Orundel and Vaelora. Established populations 24m Khazari, 18m Eldar and 31m Urakai remain unchanged. Other numbers are new planning estimates, not original confirmed censuses. The other continent and Avarra settlement gazetteers are Eryndor Living Atlas II — Avarra, Seven Thrones & Regional Settlements and Eryndor Living Atlas III — Tharvorn, Sahrad, Orundel & Vaelora. Aelwyn, Drakari and Living Mountains retain unknown exact counts. Cultural complexity and individual agency below continue to apply. ## Complete topic reference — preserved from the preceding edition This page records the established intelligent peoples, broad cultural groupings, demographic notes and the common personality reputations associated with them. These descriptions are a starting point for worldbuilding and NPC characterisation, not biological laws. ## Peoples' distinct magical traditions survive the expanded cosmology (creator clarification, 21 November 2026) Binding distinction: The creator explicitly retains the different kinds of magic long associated with Khazari (dwarves), Eldar (elves), Aelwyn Fae, fairy peoples such as Pixies, Gnomes, and other peoples. These are legitimate distinct cultural, practical, possibly innate or supernatural traditions in the setting, not merely interchangeable labels for generic lunar spells. A tradition may have customary methods, ethics, rites, materials, aptitudes and histories, but the detailed disciplines and mechanisms outside already defined Khazari examples remain to be developed—not manufactured retrospectively. Do not merge Aelwyn Fae with Pixies/fairy folk, or make Gnome magic a copy of Khazari rune systems. Individual members of any people are not required to practise any tradition; cross-cultural learning and overlapping magic are possible when consistent with training and ability. Exact already-established Khazari traditions: Runecraft (symbols and enchantments); Deepcraft (stone, earth and subterranean perception/workings); Forgebinding (magical craft and durability); Hearthmagic (warmth, preservation, protection and domestic/settlement uses); Stonecalling (rare mountain-sense/communication); Ancestral Binding (controversial bloodline, oath and hereditary work). Keep them individually distinct, not automatically all lunar or inherently benevolent. Established broad fields include Arcana, Nature, Divination, Bloodcraft, Runecraft and Shadowcraft; these are not exhaustive nor species-exclusive. Moral aspect: Some magical forces are inherently good, some morally grey and some inherently evil, regardless of the caster's intentions. Do not assign an inherent moral alignment to an entire people, civilization, cultural school or broad discipline without specific creator definition; a tradition can contain different techniques and moral natures. This distinction adds nuance to the system without erasing Fae, fairy, Gnome, Eldar, Khazari or other magical heritage. Cosmic sources and knowledge: Moons are literal sources of lunar magic and people know that fact, but not how/why or which moon creates which magical force; some moons show almost no effects, others much stronger. Eryndor independently generates Natural Magic / the World's Breath. Gods of magic can govern or interact with magical forces, not replace moon magic as its source. Do not assign individual moons to cultural traditions or claim that all folk magic derives only from lunar forces without future decisions. Historical mystery, uncertainty and the paused Gloin scene remain protected. ## Why Goblins, Ogres and Urakai face western prejudice — older war history (21 November 2026) Creator's historical explanation: During wars between eastern and western peoples in the Third Age or later, some eastern Goblin and Ogre groups fought with or aided Urakai. Long after Goblins and Ogres moved into western lands and established ordinary, numerous communities, memory of those alliances persisted as discrimination. Western Goblins are stereotyped as thieving/conniving and widely distrusted; Ogres are widely feared, in part due to fearsome wartime reputation; rare western Urakai visitors face antipathy tied to their eastern political and military associations. These are historically inherited prejudices, not innate racial traits or proof all ancestral groups took one side. Exact dates, war names, cultures and campaigns are OPEN. The creator also raised eastern origins and the possibility that Goblins/Ogres are distinct distant biological cousins of Urakai; biological kinship is NOT established. Eastern/southeastern badlands are the main current Urakai heartlands; the Eastern Grasslands have very rare Urakai and no established Urakai settlements. Western Goblins/Ogres remain commonplace. See 03 — History & Ancient Lore for the full historical and canon-status distinction. ## Western Avarra — feared Ogres versus distrusted Goblins (creator refinement, 21 November 2026) Ogres are feared across much of western Avarra. Their size, physical power and often exaggerated reputation for violence provoke genuine apprehension: guards may be visibly tense, isolated villages nervous, innkeepers reluctant and children told frightening tales. This is a social perception, not a statement that all Ogres are violent or hostile. Ogres are common western inhabitants with their own families, villages, trades, civic lives and varied personalities. Fear may lead to exclusion or unequal treatment in some places, but no uniform kingdom-wide Ogre persecution is automatically established. Goblins are distrusted, particularly on the persistent stereotypes that they are thieving, conniving, scheming or dishonest. Those prejudices cause heavy discrimination in markets, guilds, courts, property rights and everyday dealings in many western societies. Some Goblins genuinely commit crimes, as members of any other people can; the stereotype is not an innate trait or a reliable assessment of an individual. Goblins too are common established western residents, not a universally criminal, nomadic or villainous species. Different towns, governments and individuals vary greatly in how hostile or welcoming they are. This is the latest creator clarification and supersedes any previous ambiguous claim that Ogres are simply undistinguished from other commonplace western peoples or that Goblins are the only people subjected to fear or prejudice. Neither category has fixed moral alignment, and the existing sixfold population model is unchanged. ## Earlier western social interpretation — superseded where clarified above Latest creator clarification, overriding the immediately preceding broad interpretation: Both Goblins and Ogres are common, ordinary inhabitants of western Avarra, with permanent families, villages, market districts, industries, travelling households, and all sorts of jobs and social positions. Goblins specifically experience substantial, widespread discrimination in western society. This may manifest through racist folklore, exclusionary local guilds and schools, unequal trade terms, suspicious guards, restricted civic rights or property tenure, segregated neighborhoods, hostile villages and habitual stereotyping, with actual severity varying across kingdoms, courts, regions and individual communities. Some cities recognize full equal citizenship and some Goblin institutions are powerful and independent; persistent discrimination remains an important feature of the wider western social reality. A Goblin individual's morality, honesty, intellect or occupation is not determined by those prejudices. Do not transfer Goblin-specific thieving/conniving stereotypes to Ogres: Ogres are instead widely feared for their strength and perceived dangerousness, not presumed schemers. Ogres are equally legitimate and often encountered western residents, and their size may have practical or local social consequences, but the creator's 'heavily discriminated' statement was expressly about Goblins. No uniform Ogre persecution statute is established, but fear may produce varying levels of suspicion, avoidance and discrimination. Ogres may be craftsmen, scholars, soldiers, officials, farmers, haulers, parents, wanderers, merchants or outlaws as individuals, with diverse social experiences. Neither people is a comic prop, innately evil, politically unified or required to live only in western lands. Avarra's already modeled population totals are redistributed socially and regionally without adding extra individuals or changing birth rates. ## Shared principles - Eryndor contains many intelligent peoples with distinct histories, societies, customs and political interests. - No people is inherently good or evil, intelligent or foolish, civilised or savage. - Cultural reputation, species traits, individual personality and political allegiance are different things. Do not conflate them. - Individuals vary by region, family, class, profession, religion, education, upbringing, personal history and circumstance. - Some peoples are organised into kingdoms or large civilisations; others may have local, mobile, seasonal, clan-based, forest, coastal or other social structures. Do not assume every people has a conventional monarchy or state. - The sentient animal peoples are fully intelligent peoples with their own societies, not ordinary animals wearing clothes. They coexist alongside ordinary animals and livestock. An animal-like appearance alone does not establish whether a particular creature is an ordinary animal or a sentient person; establish this in context rather than assuming. - The personality descriptions below are cultural reputations and tendencies. Other peoples may misunderstand or exaggerate them. They can inform humour, prejudice, diplomacy, conflict or subversion, but they are not objective rules for every individual. ## Major ancient civilisations ### Khazari — dwarves - Current modeled population: Approximately 144 million worldwide (24 million was the superseded baseline). - Common lifespan: Approximately 300–450 years. - Political organisation: Seven powerful, culturally distinct and politically independent Mountain Thrones. - Established character: Proud, stubborn, practical, industrious and loyal. Craftsmanship, family, tradition, hard work and keeping one's word are highly respected. - Cultural tendencies: Long memories, serious grudges, dry humour, strong food and drink traditions, engineering, mining, metalwork, stonework and things built to last. - Important distinction: The Seven Thrones are not one uniform kingdom. Local law, customs, politics, dialect and identity can differ significantly. - Current campaign centre: Karak-Varn, one of the Seven Thrones. ### Eldar — elves - Current modeled population: Approximately 108 million worldwide (18 million was the superseded baseline). - Common lifespan: Approximately 700–1,200 years. - Political organisation: Several royal houses gathered under a High Sovereign in the western forests of Letharion. - Established character: Graceful, perceptive, intelligent, patient and artistic. Beauty, knowledge, history, etiquette and precision are valued. - Cultural reputation: Famously formal and exacting in manners and language. They may be exquisitely courteous while making disagreement feel like a surgical dissection. Their long memories can preserve both promises and old insults. - Variation: Some Eldar are traditionalists; others reject etiquette, speak bluntly, or use manners as political theatre. Do not make all Eldar smug, infallible or interchangeable. ### Urakai — orcs - Current modeled population: Approximately 186 million worldwide (31 million was the superseded baseline). - Political organisation: Sophisticated clan confederations across eastern plains and highlands; they are a rising civilisation. - Established character: Fierce, direct, proud, competitive and passionate. Courage, strength, endurance, loyalty and achievement are admired. - Cultural tendencies: Plain speaking, respect for those who stand their ground, strong family, clan and comrade loyalties. - Political context: Their ancient rivalry with the Khazari is political, territorial, industrial and military. Trade and alliances remain possible. - Important distinction: Urakai societies are sophisticated, not primitive, and the people are not inherently villainous. ## Other established peoples ### Drakari — true dragons - Population: Fewer than 10,000. - Organisation: Ancient courts and territories. - Common character reputation: Ancient, intelligent, proud, territorial and self-possessed. Knowledge, power, reputation, independence and ancient obligations matter to them. - Variation: Some are noble, philosophical and patient; others are vain, possessive, cruel or obsessively proud. They are individuals with histories and interests, not interchangeable monsters. ### Aelwyn — Fae - Organisation: Ancient seasonal courts and pacts. - Common character reputation: Enigmatic, whimsical, beautiful, unpredictable and deeply bound to old customs. - Cultural tendencies: Riddles, bargains, symbolism, ceremony and unusual hospitality. Promises, names, gifts and obligations may carry implications that outsiders do not understand. - Variation: Do not assume all Aelwyn are malicious or deceptive. Some may be generous, curious, solemn or sincerely devoted to their customs. ### Halflings Friendly, sociable, humble, cheerful, hospitable and fond of comfort. They value meals, family, gardens, stories, familiar places and local gossip. They may prefer peace and ordinary pleasures to danger, but can be brave, resourceful and stubborn when home or loved ones are threatened. Comfort-seeking is not cowardice. ### Gnomes Curious, inventive, clever, eccentric and inquisitive. They are drawn to mechanisms, puzzles, experiments, obscure knowledge and overlooked problems. Their ingenuity can be extraordinary, though enthusiasm can outrun caution. Some are meticulous theoreticians; others are chaotic tinkerers. ### Goblins Opportunistic, crafty, suspicious, quick-witted and resourceful. They value survival, cleverness, useful possessions, information and knowing when to retreat. They may be irreverent and fond of bargains. Goblin communities can be fiercely protective of their own; not every goblin is dishonest. ### Ents Patient, contemplative, ancient, deliberate and deeply connected to the natural world. They tend to think in seasons, generations and centuries. They protect forests and living things, may be slow to anger, and can be immense when roused. Individual temperaments still differ. ### Centaurs Independent, proud, athletic, adventurous and freedom-loving. They value open spaces, skill, kinship, personal honour and freedom of movement. They may be blunt and competitive, and impatient with cramped cities or excessive restrictions. They can be scouts, hunters, messengers, warriors, scholars, diplomats or artisans. ### Merfolk Proud, perceptive, adaptable and deeply aware of tides, currents and the changing sea. Navigation, memory, tradition, community and knowledge of the waters can be important. Some regard surface-dwellers as noisy, clumsy or ignorant of the ocean; others may be welcoming traders, curious travellers or skilled intermediaries. Their communities vary. ### Giants Powerful, independent, blunt, proud and sometimes slow to trust. They may value strength, endurance, hospitality and respect for territory. Their scale and possible longevity can shape their outlook, but do not make them simple-minded. Some are solitary and contemplative; others live in close-knit mountain or highland communities. Their size is not a personality. ## Rare colossal sentient beings ### Living Mountains Living Mountains are genuine, exceedingly rare colossal living beings. While dormant, their bodies can be indistinguishable from ordinary mountain ranges or solitary peaks. They may sleep for centuries or millennia, with forests, rivers, caves, snow and even settlements accumulating across them. Their movements and timescales are almost impossible for smaller peoples to comprehend. It is not established that they share one temperament or a common psychology. An individual might be contemplative, indifferent, protective, curious, wary or incomprehensible to smaller beings; these are possibilities for individual characterisation, not fixed species traits. They are not automatically benevolent, hostile, wise or interested in mortals. Most people will never witness one awaken, and reliable evidence is scarce. Their number, locations, origins, names and individual personalities remain unknown. Classification boundary: Living Mountains are included because they are sentient colossal life, but they are not a conventional widespread species or ordinary monster type. They are distinct from Giants and Ents. Do not make them convenient mounts or weapons, or connect one to Gloin or the eastern mine without a properly developed reason. ## Humans and the five major cultural groupings Humans are adaptable, ambitious, inventive, emotional and politically complicated. Their shorter lifespans often encourage urgency, energetic change and a desire to leave a legacy. The five major power groupings below have broad cultural reputations; none describes every human in that region. ### Aldermere Stubborn, practical, duty-bound and community-minded. They tend to admire courage, loyalty, hard work and keeping one's word. They often respect proof through action more than grand promises. ### Valtoria Disciplined, ambitious, hierarchical and politically calculating. They value order, military achievement, status, efficiency and national strength. Court and military life can be intensely competitive; personal loyalties and rivalries still matter. ### Northern Holds Hardy, blunt, resilient and cautious with outsiders until trust is earned. They value survival, kinship, hospitality, endurance and practical competence. They are not all grim or humourless. ### Merchant Republics Cunning, persuasive, cosmopolitan and commercially minded. They value opportunity, negotiation, information, wealth and recognising a good bargain. Commercial calculation does not exclude honour, generosity or sincere friendship. ### Southern Sultanates Cultured, scholarly, proud, hospitable and politically sophisticated. They value poetry, learning, trade, architecture, ceremony, reputation and refined debate. Hospitality may be elaborate; courtly life can involve subtle competition and diplomacy. These societies are not monolithic. ## Sentient animal peoples These peoples have their own families, societies, traditions and political interests. Animal traits may influence senses, instincts, movement or physical behaviour, but they are not simply animals wearing clothes. ### Wolvenkin Loyal, disciplined, protective, perceptive and community-oriented. They value trust, family, teamwork and earned respect. They may be alert to changes in their surroundings and slow to forgive betrayal. Pack-like bonds may inform social life, but not every community is organised identically. ### Foxfolk Clever, charming, curious, adaptable and mischievous. Such traditions should be attributed to their sources rather than presented as universally confirmed history. ## Roleplaying and worldbuilding guidance - Give each NPC an individual personality, motive, flaw, loyalty and history. - Species reputation is a starting expectation, not a script. - Regional culture, class, profession, faith, education, family and personal experiences all matter. - Let characters contradict stereotypes naturally. - Do not use species as a shortcut for moral alignment, intelligence or worth. - A people can have multiple societies, political factions, dialects and internal disagreements. - When developing a new people, establish its ecology, society, history and relationships without assuming it must resemble a familiar fantasy template. ## Small communities and scattered settlements Not every people in Eryndor belongs to a great kingdom, city or unified civilisation. The world should also contain small villages, hamlets, hidden steadings, burrow-settlements, woodland enclaves, cave communities and other modest homes belonging to lesser magical peoples and other small-scale communities. These settlements may be scattered across forests, woodlands, plains, hills, marshes, mountain valleys, underground passages and caverns, and suitable coastal, island or underwater environments. Some may be close to major roads or larger settlements; others may be remote, concealed, seasonal or accessible only through local knowledge. Their scale and way of life should suit the people, habitat and available resources. A settlement does not need to be a sovereign nation or have a formal ruler. It may be a family cluster, a few neighbouring households, a clan hamlet, a market village, a network of burrows or a small community connected to nearby settlements by custom, trade, kinship or mutual protection. Some communities may be mixed; others may be predominantly one people. This is established world canon. The nine additional peoples have suitable small communities where habitat, ecology and geography support them. Additional peoples beyond this roster still require explicit approval. The individual settlement patterns, named villages, locations, populations and political relationships of any approved entries remain to be developed where not already specified. Do not invent named settlements or precise map placements and present them as previously established. ## Additional peoples — established canon The following nine peoples are established inhabitants of Eryndor: Kobolds, Satyrs/Fauns, Pixies, Minotaurs, Brownies/Boggarts, Ogres, Trolls, Mushroom folk and Harpies. The descriptions and cultural concepts in this chapter are current canon and may be revised, expanded, replaced or retconned by the creator at any time. Details explicitly marked unknown or unresolved remain open; canon status does not require inventing answers to unanswered biological, historical or cultural questions. Each people includes individuals of varied character and morality. ### Kobolds — established people Core concept: Small, intelligent, scaled folk adapted to enclosed spaces, rough terrain and communal construction. They should be a real people rather than disposable trap-making nuisances. Provisional biology: Generally short, light-framed and agile, with overlapping scales, strong hands, clawed fingers and keen low-light vision. Their exact appearance may vary between lineages and regions. Their exact thermal physiology remains unresolved; whether they are fully warm-blooded or partially temperature-sensitive has not been decided. In either case, avoid making them implausibly comfortable in every climate. Their size may help in narrow passages but should limit reach, carrying capacity and direct physical contests with larger folk. Their senses, diet, reproduction and lifespan remain open. Societies: Some communities could live in natural caverns, old quarries, cliff warrens, dry ravines or carefully engineered burrow networks. Others might build surface hamlets around workshops, kilns or mines. Cooperative engineering, water management, ventilation, storage and shared maintenance could be central to some cultures, while others are pastoral, trading or itinerant. A kobold community may be meticulous and safety-conscious; another may be a chaotic collection of brilliant improvisers. Character and humour: Practical, inventive, socially observant and sometimes suspicious of outsiders. Their humour can involve elaborate warning signs, petty engineering rivalries and arguments over whose tunnel is technically the main entrance. Do not make all kobolds cowardly, greedy, trap-obsessed or obsessed with dragons. Open design questions: How closely, if at all, do they associate with Drakari? Are there major regional lineages? What are their actual thermal needs and lifespan? ### Satyrs / Fauns — established people Core concept: A people with humanlike upper bodies and caprine lower limbs, adapted to woodland margins, hills, rocky slopes and open pastoral country. Satyr and faun may be regional names, related cultural branches or two distinct peoples; that distinction is not yet decided. Provisional biology: Digitigrade legs, cloven hooves, balance suited to uneven ground, and digestive systems adapted to a mixed diet with substantial plant matter. Horns, ears, coats and body proportions may vary. Their agility should be terrain-dependent rather than supernatural: excellent on broken slopes and woodland paths, less suited to deep water, smooth floors or heavy armour. Avoid assuming every individual is musical, intoxicated or sexually mischievous. Societies: Possible forms include seasonal woodland villages, hill hamlets, orchard communities, shepherding clans, travelling performers, herbalist settlements and permanent market villages. Some may maintain carefully negotiated boundaries with farmers and forest peoples; others may be integrated into larger towns. Music, dance, storytelling, horticulture and animal husbandry can be important in some communities without defining all of them. Character and humour: Sociable traditions may coexist with serious law, land stewardship, family obligations and old grudges. A village may host exuberant seasonal festivals but take water rights, grazing boundaries and hospitality rules extremely seriously. Open design questions: Whether Satyrs and Fauns are one people or related peoples; horn variation; diet and digestive limits; family structure and lifespan. ### Pixies — established people Core concept: Very small, winged, fully intelligent people. Their small size should shape architecture, transport, food requirements and vulnerability without making them childlike or inconsequential. Provisional biology: Lightweight bodies and wings capable of powered flight over limited distances, with flight constrained by weather, fatigue, injury and carried weight. Small body mass creates high heat-loss and energy demands; frequent feeding and sheltered resting places are plausible. Wings should be biological structures with believable attachment and musculature, not effortless magical hover engines. Whether all pixies can fly, and whether wing forms vary, remains open. Societies: Small canopy settlements, hollow-tree chambers, cliff gardens, reed-bed villages, flower-meadow hamlets and concealed structures among larger settlements are possible. Their homes may use lightweight materials, woven fibres, resin, leaf structures and tiny tools. Some communities may trade in specialist knowledge, pollination services, fine craft or messages; others may avoid outsiders. Character and humour: Pixie mischief can be clever social play, protest, practical jokes or a defence against intruders—not random cruelty. A sign moved a few feet, a missing button or a traveller sent along the scenic path can be funny; stealing medicine or leading someone into mortal danger has real consequences. Pixies can also be serious historians, diplomats, gardeners or guardians. Open design questions: Wing anatomy and flight endurance; whether magic is required for flight; how they interact with Aelwyn Fae; lifespan and reproductive biology. ### Minotaurs — established people Core concept: A powerful, horned, bovine-featured people with their own complex societies. They should not be reduced to maze guardians or inherently violent brutes. Provisional biology: Large, muscular humanoid bodies with bovine heads, horns, hooves or broad cloven feet, substantial neck and shoulder musculature, and senses adapted to their environment. Horn shape may vary by lineage, sex, age or individual, but do not assume a single universal pattern. Their size and mass require substantial food, water and space; heat management and joint stress matter. Their anatomy should make clothing, tools, stairs, doorways and transport distinct from human norms. Societies: Some may build broad-street towns, fortified hill settlements, agricultural villages or stone-built communities at crossroads. Others may be mobile pastoralists or members of mixed urban populations. Architecture may favour courtyards, open halls, broad entrances and durable surfaces. Labyrinthine buildings could be cultural, defensive or ceremonial in some regions, but should not define every minotaur settlement. Character and humour: Directness, physical confidence or a reputation for being difficult to move may feature in some cultures, but individuals vary widely. A minotaur architect might be obsessed with elegant wayfinding precisely because outsiders keep assuming every building is a maze. Open design questions: Exact body size range, horn biology, diet, lifespan, birth and family patterns, and whether there are distinct regional peoples under the minotaur name. ### Brownies and Boggarts — established people; relationship unresolved Core concept: Two related small household and landscape peoples in folklore, potentially close relatives or culturally linked branches. Their exact relationship remains undecided. They must be people with agency, not invisible servants or automatic household spirits. Provisional biology: Small-bodied, largely terrestrial folk able to live in human- or dwarf-scale buildings, barns, root-cellars, hedgerows and small burrows. Adaptations may include quiet movement, excellent hearing and comfort in sheltered low-light spaces. Their biology should not require them to vanish, become intangible or work without rest. The names Brownie and Boggart may describe different lineages, local labels or social roles rather than fixed moral categories. Societies: Some Brownie communities may live in small hamlets near farms, mills, stables or villages, maintaining discreet trade and neighbourly agreements. Some Boggart communities may prefer abandoned structures, old boundary places, hedgerows or isolated homesteads. Both may have family networks, local councils, customs and their own economies. Helping with repairs or animal care should be a negotiated relationship, never an assumed obligation. Character and humour: Brownies might be proud of reliable workmanship and deeply offended by being treated as free labour. Boggarts might enjoy unsettling noises, rearranging tools or exposing a household's bad habits. Neither category is morally uniform: a brownie can be a scoundrel, a boggart a loyal neighbour. Open design questions: Whether these are biological relatives, distinct peoples or names imposed by outsiders; how visible they are; what they eat; and whether they possess any innate magic. ## Magical concealment of fairy-tale settlements — worldwide creator rule (21 November 2026) Creator-established extension of the living fairy-tale world: A large number of communities, settlements, hamlets, islands, groves, cave networks and even sizable villages or towns of Eryndor's many established intelligent peoples may be hidden through magic. Western Ogres are commonly encountered but generally feared because of old eastern-war associations and reputation for strength, while Goblins are commonly encountered but distrusted under stereotypes of theft and scheming. Neither stereotype describes every person. Continuity: These fairy-tale hamlets and swamp huts add texture to the huge settled western continent without automatically naming a new location, assigning an Ogre personality, multiplying population, connecting anyone to Gloin's ancestry, or advancing the paused campaign. An artist may place a few Ogre huts in the marshland and some Ogre civic settlements in surrounding town country; do not cover every wetland with them or portray an Ogre hut as the mandatory default for Ogre society. ### Ogres — established people Core concept: A large-bodied, intelligent people with varied communities, not a synonym for stupid monster. Provisional biology: Robust, heavy-framed humanoids with high caloric and water requirements, strong musculature and physical adaptations suited to carrying loads and traversing rough country. Their size brings trade-offs: greater food needs, difficulty with small structures, heat stress and slower recovery from some injuries. Avoid making them uniformly gigantic; a plausible range of body sizes and regional variation is preferable. Societies: Some may live in extended-family villages, mountain-valley hamlets, forest-edge settlements or river communities. Others may be integrated into larger towns as builders, quarry workers, ferrymen, farmers, guards, cooks or artisans. Their architecture and tools should be scaled to local needs, with mixed-size public spaces where communities interact with smaller peoples. Character and humour: A culture might prize generous hospitality and enormous communal meals, while another values quiet scholarship or careful craftsmanship. Humour can arise from scale mismatches and assumptions, not from making ogres stupid. A master negotiator or meticulous clockmaker is entirely possible. Open design questions: Average height and mass; diet and food production; lifespan; whether ogres are closely related to any other large peoples; and regional variation. ### Trolls — established people Core concept: A diverse people adapted to harsh, damp, rocky, cold or otherwise demanding environments. Their folklore reputation for being dangerous or difficult to kill should not become universal biology. Provisional biology: Heavy, resilient bodies with thick skin, strong connective tissue and adaptations to particular climates. Some lineages may have slow metabolisms or long periods of torpor; others may be active year-round. Regeneration, if included, must have strict biological limits, costs and failure conditions. No automatic limb regrowth or immunity to ordinary weapons. Trolls should not all turn to stone in sunlight; any light sensitivity or environmental vulnerability should be regional and specific. Societies: Bridge-side hamlets, mountain settlements, river-valley villages, cold-region steadings and cave communities are possibilities. Some may maintain toll rights, ferries, stonework, fishing grounds or seasonal grazing routes. Others may live in ordinary mixed settlements. A troll village could be known for bridge engineering, patient dispute resolution or a very strict policy about littering in the river. Character and humour: Some trolls may be taciturn and slow to trust; others sociable, scholarly or theatrical. A reputation for guarding bridges could arise from a few local customs or historical agreements, not a universal instinct. Open design questions: Which lineages, if any, regenerate; metabolism and dormancy; sunlight tolerance; lifespan; and the origins of regional troll folklore. ### Mushroom folk — established people Core concept: A people whose bodies are fungal or fungus-like, with varied forms and a life cycle fundamentally different from animal peoples. They should not be walking mushrooms with a single shared mind or personality. Provisional biology: Bodies may combine a visible fruiting structure with a more substantial living body and rootlike or mycelial tissues. They may exchange nutrients through fungal networks, symbiosis or cultivated substrates. Their needs could include moisture, minerals, organic matter and particular temperature ranges. Reproduction may involve spores, budding or other processes, but spore release should not automatically infect, control or transform other peoples. Individual identity, memory and consent must remain clear unless a specific culture or biology deliberately complicates them. Societies: Communities may grow into living architecture in damp forests, old roots, caves, wetlands and underground chambers. Some could cultivate orchards, decay fallen timber, manage soil fertility or maintain underground gardens. Their settlements might be seasonal or move slowly as their growing substrate changes. Trade could involve medicines, dyes, preserved foods, cultivation knowledge and materials. Character and humour: Some communities may be contemplative and patient; others argumentative, entrepreneurial, gossipy or extremely competitive about cultivation. A mushroom-folk village can have politics, gossip and a terrible local theatre troupe like anyone else. Open design questions: Individual lifespan and continuity; whether mycelial networks share information or consciousness; spore safety; mobility; food and water requirements; and how reproduction works. ### Harpies — established people Core concept: A winged, avian-featured intelligent people adapted to cliffs, highlands, sea stacks and open-air settlements. They are not simply bird monsters or universally predatory. Provisional biology: Humanlike or otherwise clearly sapient bodies with feathered wings, strong flight musculature, light but durable skeletons and specialised respiratory and balance systems. True powered flight imposes strict limits on body mass, wing area, take-off space and carried loads. Large individuals may glide more easily than they can take off from flat ground. Hands, feet and wing anatomy need a deliberate design decision: grasping hands plus wings are possible as fantasy biology, but should be internally consistent and affect tool use. Societies: Cliffside villages, highland hamlets, sea-stack settlements and elevated communal structures are possibilities. Their architecture may use ledges, ramps, windbreaks, rope systems and sheltered landing areas. Some may be coastal fishers, couriers, navigators, shepherds or traders; others may be settled inland communities. Ground-level access and accessibility should be considered in mixed settlements. Character and humour: Singing may be an art, work tradition or regional custom, but not an irresistible biological compulsion. Some harpies may be quiet, some terrible singers, some skilled negotiators or meticulous builders. Their reputation for shrieking or luring travellers could be folklore, propaganda or a description of particular groups—not a universal trait. Open design questions: Wing and hand anatomy; flight limits and body-size range; diet; nesting and family structures; lifespan; and whether regional forms differ substantially. ## Shared canon principles for the nine additional peoples - Kobolds, Satyrs/Fauns, Pixies, Minotaurs, Brownies/Boggarts, Ogres, Trolls, Mushroom folk and Harpies are established peoples of Eryndor. Their current concepts and descriptions are canon, subject to future revision by the creator. - Each people must have believable biology, ecological needs, reproduction and life history, with abilities balanced by meaningful constraints. - Each should contain multiple cultures, settlements, occupations, personalities and political arrangements. No single village or character represents an entire people. - Serious history, ordinary daily life, humour and eccentricity can coexist. Whimsy should not erase danger, agency, dignity or consequences. - Avoid assigning inherent morality, intelligence, temperament or political allegiance by species. - Distinguish innate biological traits from learned skills, cultural customs, magical abilities and outsider stereotypes. - Do not invent precise populations, lifespans, continent-wide ranges, moon affinities, powers or historical origins where they have not yet been established. These details remain open, but the current established traits and reputations should be used consistently unless the user revises them. - Their small villages and hamlets may occur in forests, plains, hills, mountains, underground regions, coasts and oceans where biologically and culturally plausible. No exact named settlements or coordinates are established by these drafts. - Do not silently merge these peoples with Goblins, Gnomes, Halflings, Aelwyn Fae, Merfolk, Giants, Ents or Living Mountains. Any kinship, shared ancestry or political relationship requires its own decision. ## Encounter direction — familiar fantasy danger and rarity of exceptions This section establishes the current canon direction for the nine additional peoples' reputations, behaviour and rarity of unusually kind individuals. These portrayals are part of the setting and may be revised by the creator. No species is inherently good or evil; individual and group behaviour remains grounded in motive, culture, circumstance and choice. Eryndor should retain the familiar emotional language of fantasy folklore and adventure. Readers should recognise the fears, warnings, legends and dangers associated with creatures and peoples. Do not make every familiar fantasy idea morally inverted, harmless, or so nuanced that it loses its dramatic identity. Some creatures really are dangerous; some individuals and groups are malicious; some encounters should be frightening, and retreat may be the sensible response. At the same time, a species' reputation is not an absolute rule about every individual. No species is inherently good or evil. Where trustworthy individuals are described as exceptionally rare, that rarity belongs to a particular local reputation, hostile faction, social norm or historical pattern—not to an innate moral nature shared by the whole people. Communities and individuals may be dangerous, predatory, welcoming, cooperative, cruel or generous, and those patterns can vary by region and circumstance. A rare exception can feel meaningful without turning morality into a biological trait. ### Working reputation and exception spectrum - Ogres: Often dangerous, aggressive or associated with raids on isolated settlements, livestock theft, violence and destruction. Peaceful ogre communities and decent individuals can exist without being extraordinary impossibilities; the degree of danger varies by group and individual. - Harpies: Generally feared as dangerous aerial predators or raiders. Villagers may dread flocks near roads, fields, mountain passes and livestock. A genuinely kind, reliable harpy should be exceptionally rare and likely to challenge strong assumptions. - Minotaurs: Generally intimidating and widely associated in some regions with great physical danger, violent rampages or feared clans and individuals. A peaceful, trustworthy Minotaur should be exceptionally unusual; people may reasonably be frightened or wary before knowing one. - Trolls: Often feared as dangerous, territorial and unpredictable, especially around bridges, caves, rivers and mountain paths. Some may be capable of bargains or peaceful dealings, but danger remains real. - Kobolds: May be regarded as crafty, secretive, troublesome or dangerous around mines, tunnels and warrens. They can also trade, cooperate and form friendships; do not reduce every encounter to a trap or ambush. - Pixies: May be whimsical and mischievous, but their small size should not make them automatically harmless. Pranks, misdirection and luring travellers into danger can feature in folklore and real encounters. - Boggarts: May carry a strong folklore reputation for frightening, unsettling or malicious mischief — the sort of being invoked in warnings to children about strange noises outside at night. Brownies and boggarts need not share the same reputation. - Brownies: May more commonly be associated with helpful household or farmstead folklore, while still having agency, boundaries and the capacity for resentment or wrongdoing. They are not automatic servants. - Satyrs/Fauns: May be known in some places as sociable, charming woodland or pastoral folk, while stories of dangerous invitations, mischief or threatening individuals give travellers reason for caution. - Mushroom folk: May be unfamiliar or unsettling to outsiders, with some communities welcoming and others genuinely strange, secretive or dangerous. Do not make unfamiliarity itself proof of evil. These are broad working reputations and story expectations, not universal facts about every region, settlement or individual. Local folklore may exaggerate, contradict or misunderstand what is actually true. A feared reputation should still have a plausible basis in history, behaviour, dangerous encounters or cultural memory. ### Storytelling principles - Preserve recognisable fantasy folklore: the big bad wolf in the dark woods, warnings about harpies overhead, the Minotaur that tears through a village, and the ogre that raids a farmstead should all feel at home in Eryndor where appropriate. - Do not flatten every people into moral ambiguity. Some individuals, bands, predators or hostile factions can be genuinely malicious and dangerous. - Do not make every member of a feared people evil. A rare exception can be memorable without making the wider reputation meaningless. - Let reputation have practical consequences: frightened villagers, barred gates, warnings to travellers, local customs, patrols, protective measures, rumours and prejudice. - Let the reader and characters encounter both the familiar expectation and the reality behind it. Sometimes the warning is justified; sometimes it is exaggerated; sometimes an unusual individual defies it. - Keep the distinction between intelligent peoples and non-sapient dangerous creatures clear. A frightening encounter need not always involve a person or society. - Do not assume every region has the same experience or opinion. Reputation should develop locally and historically. Guiding balance: Familiar fantasy at its heart, with enough biological, cultural and individual depth to make Eryndor feel like a living world. Nuance should enrich danger and wonder, not erase them. ## Third Age — proposed duration of 8,873 years and nine eras (creator working framework, 21 November 2026) Creator's current proposed historical scale: The Third Age lasted 8,873 years and contained nine distinct eras. Treat this as the current working Third Age framework while the creator considers and develops it. The wording “I think” leaves it open to explicit confirmation or later revision; do not portray the nine era names, exact boundaries, or internal divisions as already decided. If retained, Third Age-relative Years 1–8,873 inclusive cover the age, starting immediately after the world-shaking earthquakes that ended the Second Age in its Year 1,437. The event ending the Third Age and beginning the Fourth Age is not established. Nine eras are historical subdivisions within the Third Age and should not be mistaken for nine separate worldwide Ages or for uniform calendars used by every civilization. Continuity: The exiled dark mages created the Urakai (Orcs) sometime within the Third Age, by an as-yet-unknown method, intending to besiege Khazari strongholds and eventually attack Eldar and human kingdoms. No era number, precise Third Age year, military battle, realized conquest, or survival duration of individual mages is yet assigned. Goblins and Ogres may predate this Age; Urakai do not. The First Age's length remains unknown and it has no eras. The Second Age remains exactly 1,437 years with three eras: Awakening 321 years, Wonder 1,000 years, Fire 116 years. The present Fifth Age and the Era of Crowns (Year 3,847) remain as previously established; do not derive absolute cross-Age dates or alter the paused Gloin Hammerfeld campaign from this proposed Third Age scale.
